item.title: Low birth rates were emptying public schools. ICE deportations are now making it worse
item.description:
Low birth rates were emptying public schools. ICE deportations are now making it worse
November 6, 20265:00 AM ET
Brian Mann
Kelly Gonez, a longtime school board member in the Los Angeles Unified School District, says public school enrollment declines worsened after ICE raids escalated in the city in 2025. District officials say low birth rates and the loss of immigrant children in classrooms mean school campuses will likely have to close.
Carlos Jaramillo for NPR
hide caption
toggle caption i
Carlos Jaramillo for NPR
Catch up on what you missed with our Education newsletter, sent weekly.
LOS ANGELES — Long before the Trump administration started deporting hundreds of thousands of immigrants, many with school-age children, public schools nationwide faced a massive and accelerating drop in student enrollment caused mostly by shrinking families.
"Birth rates here in Los Angeles County have been declining for decades, which means fewer children enrolled in our schools," said Kelly Gonez, a board member in the LA Unified School District (LAUSD), the second largest in the country, which lost more than 300,000 students over the last two decades.

A mototaxi pass drives past a banner of Pope Leo XIV at Pimentel beach in Chiclayo, Peru, Thursday, Nov. 5, 2026, ahead of his planned trip to Uruguay, Argentina, and Peru from November 6 to 17.
Martin Mejia/AP
hide caption

Martin Mejia/AP
ROME — Pope Leo XIV is kicking off a three-nation tour of Latin America with a visit to Uruguay, the region's least Catholic and most secular country, three weeks after undergoing lung cancer surgery that had put the entire trip into question.
Religion
Pope Leo's cancer prognosis is 'very good,' according to outside medical experts
Leo is due to arrive in Montevideo after a 13-and-a-half hour flight from Rome. He has a packed three-day itinerary in Uruguay including a visit to a neighborhood plagued by gang violence, a Mass in Paysandú, some 375 kilometers (230 miles) from the capital, and another Mass in the city of Florida, about 100 kilometers (60 miles) away.

item.title: These are the races in the House and Senate that haven't been called yet
item.description:
Elections
These are the races in the House and Senate that haven't been called yet
November 5, 20267:03 PM ET
By
Megan Pratz
,
Rahul Mukherjee
,
Brent Jones
Loading...
Democrats are poised to have a strong majority in the upcoming Congress. The final numbers are still being determined and several races are still outstanding.
A few in California are being contested by two candidates in the same party. So it's clear which party will hold the seat, even if it's not clear who will win. Others are too close to call or there aren't enough ballots counted to know which candidate will prevail. In many places in the country, it takes a while to count votes. That's normal and expected.
Here's where things stand in the races that are waiting to be called in the House by The Associated Press:
Loading...
In the Senate, there are two races outstanding, Alaska and Mississippi. Because Alaska uses ranked choice voting and no candidate in the four-person race has achieved a 50% majority in the count, it may proceed to another round of counting later this month. Mississippi uses a more traditional electoral system but a large number of provisional ballots — called affidavit ballots in the state — are taking time to count. Less than 2,000 votes separate the top two candidates in that race.

item.title: How North Carolina Democrats flipped several House seats in historically GOP districts
item.description:

How North Carolina Democrats flipped several House seats in historically GOP districts
November 5, 20266:34 PM ET
By
Adam Wagner
Supporters watch Democratic senatorial candidate Roy Cooper speak during an election night event in Raleigh, N.C. on November 3, 2026.
A.M STEWART/AFP via Getty Images
hide caption
toggle caption i
A.M STEWART/AFP via Getty Images
The Associated Press has called five U.S. House races in North Carolina for Democrats, all of them in districts drawn to favor Republican candidates.
Of those districts, four are flipping from Republican control.
As of Thursday, the AP had called nine of the state's 14 House seats for Democrats and none for Republicans. It's a startling result for a delegation that went into Tuesday with 10 Republicans and four Democrats.
